title: DasherControl: one dashboard for your homelab

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Twelve browser tabs, one for every service in your homelab, and you still can't find the right one. Antoine built DasherControl to fix exactly that.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A dashboard organized around workspaces. A workspace is like a desk: you arrange applets on it, which are bookmarks and embedded applications, and keep a few Docker controls within reach.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Vue on the front, and Rust with Rocket and Diesel on the back. Behind the dashboard there are two clean paths. Saving a layout goes through workspace handlers into database records.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Container actions. When you restart a container, the request goes through an adapter called Shiplift straight to Docker. The database never touches Docker, and an applet isn't a running container. Keeping those paths apart makes the design easy to reason about.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do workspaces know who they belong to?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Each workspace has an owner. The handler reads the user's identifier from a token, lists that person's workspaces, and checks the owner before returning the applets inside. So a saved layout belongs to a user, and every applet belongs to a workspace.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: One file wraps the Shiplift calls: list containers and images, pull images, create containers, stop or restart them. That keeps the workspace model separate from Docker operations.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Can you embed any web app in an applet?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Many, through iframes. Some apps restrict embedding, so a plain external link sits alongside for those.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The page has a screenshot and the original demo recording showing workspaces and applets in action. The architecture note and the source are linked from the write-up.
